recipes.summary: Kyphi is an incense, not an oil: pleasing to the gods, and much used by the priests in Egypt. Raisins are ground with aged wine and myrrh, mixed with the other ingredients pounded and sifted, and left for a day. Honey boiled until glue-like is mixed with melted resin, the rest is worked in, and the kyphi is stored in an earthenware vessel.

recipes.greek: κῦφι θυμιάματός ἐστι σκευασία κεχαρισμένη θεοῖς· χρῶνται δὲ αὐτῷ κατακόρως οἱ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ ἱερεῖς. μείγνυται δὲ καὶ ἀντιδότοις, καὶ ἀσθματικοῖς δίδοται ἐν ποτήμασι. σκευασίαι δὲ αὐτοῦ ἐμφέρονται πλείονες, ἐν αἷς ἐστι καὶ αὕτη· κυπέρου ἡμίξεστον, ἀρκευθίδος ἁδρᾶς τὸ αὐτό, σταφίδος λιπαρᾶς ἐκγεγιγαρτισμένης μνᾶς δεκαδύο, ῥητίνης ἀποκεκαθαρμένης μνᾶς πέντε, καλάμου ἀρωματίτου, ἀσπαλάθου, σχοίνου, ἑκάστου μνᾶν μίαν, σμύρνης δραχμὰς δεκαδύο, οἴνου παλαιοῦ ξέστας ἐννέα, μέλιτος μνᾶς δύο. ἐκγιγαρτίσας τὴν σταφίδα 2 κόψον καὶ λέανον μετὰ τοῦ οἴνου καὶ τῆς σμύρνης καὶ τὰ ἄλλα κόψας καὶ σήσας μεῖξον τούτοις ἔασόν τε συμπιεῖν ἡμέραν μίαν· εἶτα ἑψήσας τὸ μέλι ἄχρι κολλώδους συστάσεως μεῖξον ἐπιμελῶς τὴν ῥητίνην τετηκυῖαν, εἶτα τὰ λοιπὰ συνανατρίψας ἐπιμελῶς ἀποτίθεσο εἰς ἀγγεῖον ὀστράκινον.
recipes.english:
Kyphi is an incense preparation pleasing to the gods, and the priests in Egypt use it in abundance. It is also mixed into antidotes and given in drinks to those with asthma. Several recipes for it are current, including the following: half a xestes of cyperus; the same quantity of large juniper berries; twelve mnai of plump raisins with their seeds removed; five mnai of purified resin; one mna each of aromatic reed, aspalathos, and rush; twelve drachmai of myrrh; nine xestai of aged wine; and two mnai of honey.

Remove the seeds from the raisins, chop them, and grind them smooth with the wine and myrrh. Pound and sift the other ingredients, mix them with this paste, and leave everything to steep together for one day. Then boil the honey to a glue-like consistency and carefully mix in the melted resin. Finally, thoroughly rub the remaining mixture together with these and store it in an earthenware vessel.

recipes.greek: ἔλαιον πρὸς τὴν ἐν ὑγιείᾳ χρῆσιν ἄριστον τὸ ὠμοτριβές, ὃ καὶ ὀμφάκινον καλοῦσι. καὶ τούτου διαφέρει τὸ νέον, ἄδηκτον, εὐῶδες· χρήσιμον δὲ τὸ τοιοῦτον καὶ εἰς τὴν τῶν μυρων κατασκευήν. ἔστι δὲ καὶ εὐστόμαχον διὰ τὸ στύφε ειν καὶ οὔλων σταλτικὸν καὶ ὀδόντων διακρατυντικὸν κρατούμενον ἐν τῷ στόματι ἱδρώτων τε ἐφεκτικόν. τὸ δὲ λιπαρώτερον καὶ παλαιὸν εἰς τὴν τῶν χαλαστικῶν φαρμάκων χρῆσιν εὔθετον. κοινῶς δὲ πᾶν ἔλαιον θερμαντικόν ἐστι καὶ μαλακτικὸν τῆς σαρκός, δυσπερίψυκτα φυλάσσον τὰ σώματα καὶ ἑτοιμότερα πρὸς τὰς ἐνεργείας ποιοῦν. 2 ἔστι δὲ καὶ εὐκοίλιον καὶ μαλακτικὸν ἀμβλῦνόν τε τὰς τῶν ἑλκούντων φαρμάκων δυνάμεις· δίδοται δὲ καὶ πρὸς τὰ θανάσιμα συνεχῶς πινόμενον καὶ ἐξεμούμενον. καθαίρει δὲ ὅσον κοτύλη σὺν πτισάνης χυλῷ ἴσῳ ποθὲν ἢ ὕδατι, στροφουμένοις τε ἐν ποτῷ ὠφελίμως δίδοται μετὰ πηγάνου ἑψηθὲν θερμὸν κυάθων ἓξ πλῆθος ἕλμεις τε ἐκβάλλει, ἐνίεταί τε τὸ αὐτὸ μάλιστα πρὸς τοὺς εἰλεώδεις. τὸ δὲ παλαιὸν θερμαντικώτερον καὶ διαφορητικώτερον, πρὸς ὀξυδερκίαν τε ὑπάλειμμα. μιμητέον δὲ εἰ μὴ παρείη τὸ παλαιὸν ἔλαιον οὕτως· κατεράσας εἰς ἀγγεῖον τοῦ παρόντος τὸ κρεῖσσον ἕψε, ἕως οὗ σχῇ μέλιτος πάχος, καὶ χρῶ· τὴν γὰρ αὐτὴν τῷ προειρημένῳ εἰσφέρεται δύναμιν.
recipes.english:
1. For maintaining health, raw-pressed oil—the kind also called omphakinon—is best. Among such oils, the fresh, non-acrid, fragrant kind is superior; oil of this sort is also useful in preparing perfumes. Its astringency makes it beneficial to the stomach. When held in the mouth, it contracts the gums and strengthens the teeth, and it also checks perspiration. The more unctuous, aged oil is suitable for use in relaxing remedies. In general, every olive oil warms and softens the flesh, protects the body from being readily chilled, and makes it readier for activity.

2. It also makes evacuation easy and softens the bowels, while blunting the capacities of medicines that cause ulceration. It is administered against deadly poisons by repeatedly drinking it and vomiting it back up. It produces a purge when a cotyle is taken with an equal measure of barley-gruel liquid or water. For people suffering intestinal griping, six cyathoi boiled with rue are beneficially given warm as a drink. This also expels intestinal worms, and the same preparation is administered by enema, especially in cases of intestinal obstruction. Aged oil is more warming and more dispersive, and it is used as an ointment to sharpen vision. If aged oil is unavailable, it should be imitated as follows: pour the best available oil into a vessel and boil it until it acquires the consistency of honey, then use it, since it supplies the same capacity as the oil described above.

recipes.summary: Pale, young olive oil is whitened in the sun. It is set out in a wide earthenware vessel and beaten with a ladle each day so that it changes and foams; on the eighth day soaked fenugreek and split resinous pine go in for eight days more. The oil is then drawn off and stored over dried melilot and iris, or, if it is not yet white, sunned and worked again.

recipes.greek: λευκαίνεται δὲ ἔλαιον οὕτως· λαβὼν τὸ τῇ χρόᾳ μὲν λευκὸν τὴν ἡλικίαν δὲ μὴ πλέον ἐνιαυσίου ἔγχεε εἰς κεραμεοῦν ἀγγεῖον πλατύστομον καινόν — ἔστωσαν δὲ μέτρῳ κοτύλαι ἑκατόν —, εἶτα θεὶς ὑφ᾿ ἥλιον ἀνάχει κόγχῳ καθ᾿ ἑκάστην ἡμέραν κατὰ τὸ μέσον, ὑψόθεν τῇ καταφορᾷ χρώμενος, ἵνα τῇ συνεχεῖ κυκήσει καὶ πληγῇ μεταβάλληται καὶ ἀφρίσῃ. τῇ δὲ ὀγδόῃ 4 ἡμέρᾳ βρέξας τήλεως καθαρᾶς δραχμὰς πεντήκοντα ἐν ὕδατι θερμῷ ἔμβαλε μαλακὴν γενομένην εἰς τὸ προειρημένον ἔλαιον χωρὶς τοῦ στραγγίσαι τὸ ὕδωρ· προσαπόδος δὲ καὶ δαλὸν πιτυίνης ὡς ὅτι λιπαρωτάτης καὶ εἰς λεπτὰ κατεσχισμένης τὰς ἴσας ὁλκὰς καὶ οὕτως ἔασον ἄλλας ὀκτὼ ἡμέρας διελθεῖν. μετὰ ταύτας δὲ ἀνάχει τῷ κόγχῳ τὸ ἔλαιον, τό τε λοιπόν, εἰ μὲν εἵη τοῦ τέλους τετευχός, εἰς καινὸν ἀγγεῖον προκεκλυσμένον οἴνῳ παλαιῷ κατεράσας ἀποτίθεσο, προυπεστρωμένων μελιλώτου στεφανίσκων αὔων ὁλκῶν ἕνδεκα καὶ ἴρεως τῆς ἴσης. εἰ δὲ μή, πάλιν ἐν ἡλίῳ θετέον αὐτὸ καὶ ἐργαστέον, ἄχρις οὗ λευκὸν γένηται.
recipes.english:
Oil is whitened as follows. Take oil that is pale in color and no more than a year old, and pour it into a new, wide-mouthed earthenware vessel; the measured quantity should be one hundred cotylai. Set it in the sun and each day lift the oil with a ladle from the center, pouring it back down from high above, so that the continual agitation and beating cause it to change and foam.

4. On the eighth day, soak fifty drachmas of clean fenugreek in warm water. When it has softened, put it into the oil described above without draining away the water. Also add an equal weight of a pine firebrand, taken from the most resinous pine possible and split into fine pieces. Leave it in this state for another eight days. When those days have passed, draw off the oil with the ladle. If it has reached the desired result, pour it into a new vessel that has previously been rinsed with aged wine, after first laying in the bottom eleven holkai of dried melilot garlands and an equal quantity of iris; then store it. If it has not succeeded, set it in the sun again and continue working it until it becomes white.

recipes.english: 5. Sicyonian oil can also be prepared from the oil described above as follows. Pour one chous of fresh, pale, raw-pressed oil and half a chous of water into a wide-mouthed, tin-lined cauldron. Boil it over a gentle fire, stirring slowly. Once it has boiled up twice, withdraw the fire from beneath it; when it has cooled, ladle off the oil. Then add more water, bring it to the boil again together with the oil, perform the remaining steps as indicated above, and store it. This oil is prepared chiefly in Sicyonia and is called Sicyonian oil. It has a moderately warming capacity and is suitable in fevers and afflictions involving the sinews. Women also use it [on the face] to produce a sheen.

recipes.summary: Olive-honey is not made: in the region of Palmyra in Syria it flows of itself from the trunks of olive trees. The text gives no preparation, only a dose and its effects.
recipes.greek: ἐλαιόμελι κατὰ Πάλμυρα τῆς Συρίας ἐκ τοῦ στελέχους ἐλαιῶν μέλιτος παχύτερον ῥεῖ, γλυκὺ τῇ γεύσει, ὅπερ πινόμενον πλῆθος κυάθων δυεῖν μετὰ κοτύλης μιᾶς ὕδατος ἄγει κατὰ κοιλίαν ὠμὸν καὶ χολῶδες. ἔννωθροι δὲ γίνονται καὶ ἔκλυτοι οἱ λαμβάνοντες, ὅπερ οὐ δεῖ εὐλαβεῖσθαι, διεγείρειν δὲ αὐτοὺς μὴ ἐῶντας καταφέρεσθαι.

Those who take it become sluggish and weak, but this should not cause alarm; they should instead be kept awake and not allowed to lapse into sleep.

recipes.english: Castor oil is prepared in the following way. Take as many ripe castor seeds as you think fit, spread them out like produce on a drying floor, and dry them in the sun until the surrounding husk splits off and falls away. Gather the kernels, put them into a mortar, and pound them thoroughly. Place them in a tin-lined cauldron containing water and bring it to the boil over a fire. When they have released all their moisture, remove the cauldron from the fire, skim off the oil floating on top with a spoon, and store it.

recipes.summary: The Egyptians, who need castor oil in abundance, make it another way. The cleaned seeds are ground in a mill, and the meal is put into baskets and pressed out.
recipes.greek: οἱ δὲ Αἰγύπτιοι διὰ τὸ δαψιλοῦς 2 χρῄζειν ἑτέρως αὐτὸ σκευάζουσι· μετὰ γὰρ τὸ καθᾶραι εἰς μύλην ἀποδόντες τοὺς κρότωνας ἀλήθουσιν ἐπιμελῶς, εἰς τὰς σφυρίδας δὲ ἐμβαλόντες τὸ ἀληλεσμένον δι᾿ ὀργάνου ἐκθλίβουσιν. ὥριμοι δέ εἰσιν οἱ κρότωνες, ὅταν ὑπὸ τῶν περιεχόντων αὐτοὺς σφαιρίων ἀπολύωνται. ποιεῖ δὲ τὸ κίκινον πρὸς ψώρας καὶ ἀχῶρας καὶ τὰς ἐν ἕδρᾳ φλεγμονάς, πρός τε ὑστέρας μύσεις καὶ διαστροφάς, ἔτι δὲ οὐλὰς ἀπρεπεῖς καὶ ὠταλγίας, ἐμπλάστροις τε μιγὲν ἐμπρακτοτέρας αὐτὰς ἐργάζεται. ἄγει δὲ καὶ κατὰ κοιλίαν ὑδατῶδες ποθέν, ἐκκρίνει δὲ καὶ ἕλμινθας.
recipes.english:
Because the Egyptians require it in abundance, they prepare it differently. After cleaning the castor seeds, they deliver them to a mill and grind them thoroughly. They then put the ground material into baskets and press it out with an implement. Castor seeds are ripe when they come free from the capsules enclosing them.

Castor oil is effective for scabies, scalp eruptions, inflammations around the anus, closure and displacement of the uterus, disfiguring scars, and earache. When mixed into plasters, it makes them more effective. When drunk, it also carries watery matter down through the bowels and expels intestinal worms.

recipes.greek: ἀμυγδάλινον ἔλαιον, ὅ τινες μετώπιον καλοῦσι, σκευάζεται οὕτως· ἀμυγδάλων πικρῶν χοίνικας τέσσαρας καθάρας καὶ ξηράνας κόψον ὑπέρῳ ξυλίνῳ ἐν ὅλμῳ κούφως, μέχρι μᾶζα γένηται, ἐπιχέας τε ζεστοῦ ὕδατος κοτύλας δύο ἔασον συμπιεῖν ἡμιώριον, ἀφ᾿ ἧς πάλιν βιαιότερον τρῖβε. εἶτα ἀποθλίβων πρὸς πλάκα ἐξίπου καὶ τὸ ἀπὸ τῶν δακτύλων εἰς μύακα ἀναλάμβανε, εἶτα πάλιν εἰς τὸ ἀποτεθλιμμένον κοτύλην μίαν ὕδατος ἐπιχέας καὶ συμπιεῖν ἐάσας τὸ αὐτὸ ποίει· ἀποδίδωσι δὲ κοτύλην μίαν τὸ τετραχοίνικον. ποιεῖ δὲ πρὸς τὰς ἐν μήτρᾳ ἀλγηδόνας καὶ πνίγας ὑστερικὰς 2 διαστροφάς τε καὶ φλεγμονὰς τῶν αὐτῶν τόπων, ἔτι δὲ κεφαλαλγίας καὶ ὤτων πόνους καὶ ἤχους καὶ συριγμούς· ὠφελεῖ δὲ καὶ νεφριτικοὺς καὶ δυσουριῶντας, λιθιῶντας, ἀσθματικοὺς καὶ σπληνικοὺς. αἴρει δὲ καὶ σπίλους ἐκ προσώπου καὶ ἐφήλεις καὶ ῥυτίδας μέλιτι μειγνύμενον καὶ κρίνου ῥίζῃ καὶ κυπρίνῃ ἢ ῥοδίνῃ κηρωτῇ, καὶ ἀμβλυωπίας δέ ἐστιν ἀνασκευαστικόν. σὺν οἴνῳ δὲ ἀχῶρας καὶ πίτυρα σμήχει.
recipes.english:
The oil of almonds—also known to some as metopion—is made in the following manner. Take four choinikes of bitter almonds, clean and dry them, and gently crush them in a mortar with a wooden pestle until they become a paste. Add two kotylai of hot water, allow the paste to absorb it for half an hour, and then grind it again, this time more vigorously. Next, press it out against a board little by little, collecting what adheres to your fingers into a spoon. Then pour one kotyle of water onto the pressed mass, allow it to be absorbed, and repeat the same process. Four choinikes yield one kotyle.

It is effective for pains in the uterus, uterine suffocation, displacement and inflammation of the same parts, as well as headache, ear pain, noises in the ears, and whistling sounds. It also benefits those with kidney disorders, difficulty urinating, stones, asthma, and disorders of the spleen. When mixed with honey, lily root, and either kypros cerate or rose cerate, it removes marks, sunspots, and wrinkles from the face; it is also remedial for dimness of sight. With wine, it cleans away scalp eruptions and dandruff.

recipes.english:
Myrtle oil is prepared as follows. Take the tender leaves of black myrtle, either wild or cultivated, pound them, and press them. Mix unripe-olive oil equal in quantity to the juice and warm it over coals until the two have boiled together, removing what rises to the surface. An easier preparation is to pound the tender leaves, boil them with water and oil, and skim off what rises. An ordinary method is to put the leaves into oil and let them steep in the sun. Some first make the oil astringent with pomegranate rinds, cypress, cyperus, and rush.

The more effective oil is somewhat bitter and oily to the taste, green, translucent, and fragrant with myrtle. It has an astringent and hardening capacity. Consequently, it is mixed with cicatrizing remedies and is also effective for burns, scaly affections, dandruff, eruptions, chafing sores, fissures, knobby growths, loosened joints, sweating, and everything that requires astringency or contraction.

recipes.english:
Bay oil is prepared from bay berries once they are ripe on the tree, by boiling them with water. The skin surrounding them releases an oily substance; after breaking it up with their hands, they gather it into a mussel shell. Others make omphacine oil astringent with cyperus, rush, and calamus, then add bay leaves and boil the mixture together. Others add bay berries as well, until the oil becomes sufficiently fragrant, while some also mix in storax and myrtle. Mountain bay and broad-leaved bay are best for the preparation.

Fresh bay oil is superior: it is green in color, extremely bitter, and pungent. It has a warming, softening, opening, and fatigue-relieving capacity. It is suitable for every disorder affecting the sinews, as well as for shivering fits, earache, catarrhs, and headache. When drunk, however, it also causes nausea.

1. Take five litrai and eight ounces of rush and twenty litrai and five ounces of oil. Chop the rush, knead it with water, and boil it while stirring; then strain. Put into the twenty litrai and five ounces of oil the petals from one thousand roses, without first wetting them. Coat your hands with fragrant honey and stir repeatedly, pressing gently. Leave it overnight and then press it out. Once the sediment has settled, transfer the oil to another receiving vessel and store it in a mixing bowl coated with honey. Place the pressed rose petals in a small washing basin, pour over them eight litrai and three ounces of the oil that has been made astringent, and press them out again.

2. This will give you the second oil. If you wish, continue pouring oil over the petals and pressing them out through a third and a fourth steeping; in this way first, second, third, and fourth grades of the perfume are produced. Whenever you do this, first coat the mixing bowls with honey. If you wish to make a second addition of petals, put the same number of fresh, unwetted rose petals into the oil from the first pressing. Stir them with hands previously coated with honey, press them out, and produce the second, third, and fourth oils by pressing in the same way. Each time you do this, add fresh roses, since the oil becomes more potent.

3. The oil can receive additions of rose petals through a seventh steeping, but no further. The pressing vat too should be coated with honey. The oil must be separated carefully from the rose juice, since even the smallest amount left mixed with it spoils the perfume. Some people crush the roses alone, steep them in oil, and replace them every seven days; after the third steeping they store the oil in this form. Others first make the oil astringent by adding calamus and aspalathos; some also add alkanet to give it an attractive color and salt to prevent spoilage.

4. It has an astringent and cooling capacity and is suitable for wet dressings and mixtures used in poultices. When given as a drink, it loosens the bowels and quenches burning in the stomach. It also promotes the filling in of hollow ulcers, soothes malignant ulcers, serves as an ointment for scurf and eruptions, as a wet dressing at the onset of headache, and as a rinse for toothache. Applied as an ointment, it is also effective for hardened eyelids; administered by irrigation, it is useful for irritations of the intestines and inflammations of the uterus.

recipes.english:
Take nine litrai of fenugreek, five litrai of olive oil, one litra of aromatic reed, and two litrai of cyperus. Steep them in the oil for seven days, stirring three times each day; then press out the oil and store it. Some steep cardamom with it instead of the aromatic reed and balsam wood instead of the cyperus. Others first render the oil astringent with these ingredients, then steep the fenugreek in it and press it out.

It has the capacity to soften abscesses and bring them to coction. It is especially suitable for every induration around the uterus. It is used as an instillation for women in difficult labor when the parts have become completely dry because the fluids were discharged beforehand, and also for inflammations of the anus. It is beneficially administered as an enema for tenesmus. It scours away dandruff and scurf; combined with wax, it benefits burns and chilblains. It also scours away freckles and is mixed into preparations for beautifying the complexion. Choose oil that is fresh, does not display the smell of fenugreek too strongly, cleanses the hands, and has a bittersweet taste, for this kind is best.

recipes.english:
Take wild thyme, cassia, southernwood, water-mint flowers, myrtle leaves, and marjoram, choosing the amount of each by estimation with due regard for its capacity. Pound everything together in the same vessel and pour on enough oil of unripe olives that the oil does not overpower the capacity of the ingredients steeped in it. Leave it for four days and press it out. Then steep the same quantity of the same ingredients, now fresh, for the same length of time, and press them out; the oil is more potent when prepared in this way. Choose oil that is dark olive in color, smells strongly of marjoram, and is moderately pungent.

2. It has a warming, attenuating, and pungent capacity. It is effective for closure and displacement of the uterus, draws down the menses and afterbirth, revives women suffering from uterine suffocation, and soothes pains of the lower back and groin. It is better to use it with honey, since it astringes the parts so strongly that it hardens them. When rubbed on, it also relieves fatigue. It is suitably mixed into poultices for those with opisthotonus and for others suffering from spasms.

recipes.greek: ὠκιμίνον σκευασία· τοῦ εἰς τὸ κύπρινον ἠρωματισμένου, ὡς ἀποδείξομεν (I 55), λαβὼν ἐλαίου λίτρας εἴκοσι, ὠκίμου σταθμῷ λίτρας ἕνδεκα οὐγγίας ὀκτὼ ἀποφυλλίσας ἀπόβρεχε νύκτα καὶ ἡμέραν ἐν τῷ ἐλαίῳ, εἶτα ἐξίπου καὶ ἀποτίθεσο. ἐκκενώσας δὲ τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς κυρτίδος ἐπίχει πάλιν τὸ ἴσον πλῆθος τοῦ ἐλαίου καὶ ἐξίπου. καλεῖται δὲ τοῦτο δευτερεῖον· τρίτην γὰρ οὐκ ἐπιδέχεται βροχήν. εἶτα προσφάτου ὠκίμου λαβὼν τὸ ἴσον πάλιν ἀπόβρεχε, ὡς ἐπὶ τοῦ ῥοδίνου εἴρηται (I 43), τὸ δὲ ἤδη ἀποβεβρεγμένον ἐπιχέων καὶ ἐῶν τὸν αὐτὸν χρόνον ἔκθλιβε καὶ ἀποτίθεσο. κἂν τρὶς δὲ ἢ τετράκις θέλῃς, ἀπόβρεχε πρόσφατον ἀεὶ ὤκιμον ἐμβάλλων. δύναται δὲ καὶ ἐκ τοῦ ὀμφοκίνου σκευάζεσθαι· βέλτιον δὲ ἐκείνως. δύναται δὲ τὸ αὐτὸ τῷ σαμψουχίνῳ, ἔλαττον ἐνεργοῦν.
recipes.english:
Take twenty litrai of the oil aromatized for making henna oil, as we shall explain below (I 55). Strip basil leaves amounting by weight to eleven litrai and eight ounces, and steep them in the oil for one night and one day; then press out the oil and store it. Empty the material from the straining basket, pour the same quantity of oil over it again, and press it out. This is called the second-grade oil, since the material will not admit a third steeping.

Next take the same quantity of fresh basil and steep it again, as stated for rose oil (I 43), pouring over it the oil already used for steeping. Leave it for the same length of time, then press it out and store it. If you wish, you may steep it three or four times, always adding fresh basil. It can also be prepared from oil of unripe olives, but the former method is better. It can accomplish the same things as marjoram oil, though it acts less strongly.

recipes.english: Into nine litrai and five ounces of the oil aromatized for making henna oil, put eight litrai of southernwood leaves. Steep them for one night and one day, then press out the oil. If you wish to make it with repeated infusions, remove the first leaves, add other leaves, steep them in the oil, and press it out. It has a warming capacity, effective for closures and indurations in the uterus, and it brings down the menses and afterbirth.

recipes.english: Steep eleven litrai and eight ounces of dill flowers for one day in eight litrai and nine ounces of olive oil. Then press them out with your hands and store the oil. If you wish to make a double-infusion oil, steep fresh dill flowers in the same way. It can soften and open the parts around the uterus. It is suitable for recurrent chills, warms the body and relieves fatigue, and benefits pains in the joints.

recipes.summary: Oil is first made astringent: boiled with calamus and myrrh in fragrant wine, strained, then steeped with soaked cardamom and pressed. The same petals are pressed twice more with fresh oil and cardamom for lesser grades; fresh lilies make the oil stronger, and it is finished with myrrh, cinnamon and saffron.

recipes.greek: σουσίνου σκευασία, ὃ ἔνιοι λείρινον καλοῦσιν ἐλαίου λίτρας ἐννέα οὐγγίας πέντε, καλάμου λίτρας πέντε οὐγγίας δέκα, σμύρνης δραχμὰς πέντε φυράσας οἴνῳ εὐώδει ἕψε, εἶτα ἀπηθήσας τὸ ἔλαιον ἀπόχει κατὰ καρδαμώμου κεκομμένου καὶ βεβρεγμένου ὕδατι ὀμερίῳ λιτρῶν τριῶν οὐγγιῶν ἓξ καὶ ἐάσας βραχῆναι ἀπόθλιβε· καὶ λαβὼν ἐκ τοῦ ἐστυμμένου ἐλαίου τρεῖς ἥμισυ λίτρας, κρίνα ἀριθμῷ χίλια ἀποφυλλίσας θὲς ἐν λουτῆρι πλατεῖ, μὴ βαθεῖ, ἐπιχέας τε τὸ ἔλαιον ἀνακίνει ταῖς χερσὶ μέλιτι κεχρισμέναις. ἐάσας δὲ ἡμέραν μίαν καὶ νύκτα, πρωὶ δὲ ἀνελόμενος εἰς κυρτίδα ἐξίπου. 2 τὸ δὲ φερόμενον ἀπήθει εὐθέως ἀπὸ τοῦ συνεκθλιβέντος ὕδατος τῷ ἐλαίῳ· οὐ γὰρ ὑπομένει ὡς τὸ ῥόδινον, συνθερμαινόμενον δὲ ἀναζεῖ καὶ σήπεται. μετάγγιζε δὲ πλεονάκις εἰς ἕτερα ἀγγεῖα μέλιτι κατακεχρισμένα, προσπάσσων ἅλας λεπτοὺς καὶ τὴν συλλεγομένην ἀκαθαρσίαν ἐπιμελῶς ἀφαιρῶν. μετεράσας δὲ ἐκ τοῦ κυρτιδίου τὸ ἐξιπωθὲν ἄρωμα εἰς τὸν λουτῆρα πάλιν ἐπίχει τοῦ ήρωματισμένου ἐλαίου τὸ ἴσον πλῆθος τῷ προτέρῳ καὶ καρδαμώμου κεκομμένου συνέμβαλε ὁλκὰς δέκα, καὶ ἀνακινήσας χρησίμως ταῖς χερσὶ καὶ ἐπισχὼν μικρὸν ἐξίπου, τὸ ἀπορρέον ἀποκαθαίρων. 3 καὶ τρίτον ἐπιχέας πάλιν τὸ αὐτὸ ποίει, προσεπεμβάλλων καὶ τὸ καρδάμωμον καὶ τοὺς ἅλας ὁμοίως καὶ τὰς χεῖρας μέλιτι χρίων καὶ θλίβων. καὶ ἔσται τὸ μὲν πρῶτον ἐκπιεσθὲν ἄριστον, ἐχόμενον δὲ τὸ ἑξῆς, τρίτον δὲ τὸ τελευταῖον. καὶ πάλιν λαβὼν χίλια κρίνα καὶ ἀποφυλλίσας διάθες καὶ ἐπιχέας τὸ πρῶτον ἐξιπωθὲν μεθόδευε, τὰ αὐτὰ ποιῶν ὥσπερ ἐποίεις ἐπὶ τοῦ πρώτου, καρδάμωμον παραμίσγων, εἶτα ἐξίπου καὶ ποίει τὰ αὐτὰ ἐπὶ τοῦ δευτέρου καὶ τρίτου, ὡς εἴρηται, προσεμβάλλων καὶ τὸ καρδάμωμον, καὶ ὁσάκις ἂν ἀποβρέξῃς νεαρὰ κρίνα, δυναμικώτερον ἕξεις τὸ μύρον. 4 ἐπὶ τέλει δὲ ὅταν αὐτάρκως ἔχειν σοι δοκῇ, μίσγε ἐν ἑκάστῃ σκευασίᾳ σμύρνης χρηστῆς δραχμὰς δύο, κιναμώμου δραχμὰς δύο, κρόκου δραχμάς δέκα. οἱ δέ· κρόκου καὶ κιναμώμου τὸ ἴσον κόψας σήσας ἔμβαλε εἰς τὸν λουτῆρα μεθʼ ὕδατος καὶ ἐπίχει τὸ πρῶτον ἐκπιεσθὲν μύρον, εἶτα ἐάσας μικρὸν ἀναλάμβανε εἰς ἀγγεῖα ξηρά, προκεχρισμένα κόμμει καὶ σμύρνῃ καὶ κρόκῳ καὶ μέλιτι μεθʼ ὕδατος διειμένοις· τὸ δʼ αὐτὸ ποίει καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ δευτέρου ἐκπιέσματος καὶ τοῦ τρίτου.
recipes.english:
1. Preparation of susinon, which some call leirinon. Mix nine litrai and five ounces of oil, five litrai and ten ounces of calamus, and five drachmai of myrrh with fragrant wine, and boil them. Then filter the oil and pour it over three litrai and six ounces of cardamom that has been chopped and soaked in rainwater. Let it steep, then press it out. Take three and a half litrai of the expressed oil; strip the petals from one thousand lilies and place them in a broad, shallow basin. Pour the oil over them and stir with hands previously coated with honey. Leave them for one day and one night; in the morning, transfer them to a straining basket and press them out.

2. Immediately filter the liquid that comes away, separating the oil from the water expressed with it. Unlike rose perfumed oil, this oil does not tolerate the water: when heated together with it, it bubbles up and spoils. Decant it several times into other vessels previously coated with honey, sprinkling it with finely ground salt and carefully removing the impurities that collect. Transfer the pressed aromatic material from the straining basket back into the basin. Pour over it the same quantity of aromatized oil as before and add ten holkai of chopped cardamom. Work it thoroughly with your hands, wait a short while, and press it out, removing impurities from the liquid that runs off.

3. Pour aromatized oil over the material a third time and repeat the same procedure, again adding the cardamom and the salt, coating your hands with honey, and pressing. The first expression will be the finest, the next one second in quality, and the last one third. Then take another thousand lilies, strip off their petals, and spread them out. Pour the first expression over them and process them just as you did the first set, mixing in cardamom, and then press them out. Treat the second and third expressions in the same way, as stated, adding cardamom as well. The more often you steep fresh lilies in it, the stronger your perfumed oil will become.

4. Finally, when you think it is sufficiently strong, mix into each preparation two drachmai of good myrrh, two drachmai of cinnamon, and ten drachmai of saffron. Others proceed as follows: pound and sift equal quantities of saffron and cinnamon, put them into the basin with water, and pour the first expression of perfumed oil over them. After leaving it briefly, transfer it into dry vessels previously coated with gum, myrrh, saffron, and honey thinned with water. Do the same with the second and third expressions.

steps.title: Make the astringent oil
steps.text: Mix 9 lb 5 oz of oil, 5 lb 10 oz of calamus and 5 drachmas of myrrh with fragrant wine and boil them. Strain off the oil.

steps.title: Steep the cardamom
steps.text: Chop 3 lb 6 oz of cardamom and soak it in rainwater. Pour the strained oil over it, let it steep, and press it out.

note.label: Made astringent
note.text: The Greek calls this oil “made astringent” (ἐστυμμένον) when it is used next; the English says “expressed”. Saffron oil (1.54) starts from the same oil.

steps.title: Steep the lilies
steps.text: Strip the petals from a thousand lilies and lay them in a broad, shallow basin. Pour 3½ lb of the prepared oil over them and stir with hands coated with honey. Leave them for a day and a night.

note.label: Broad, not deep
note.text: The petals lie spread out; the text says “spread them out” of the second thousand.

steps.title: Press, separate, decant
steps.text: In the morning put them in a straining basket and press them out. At once separate the oil from the water pressed out with it: unlike rose oil, this oil does not tolerate the water, and warmed with it, it bubbles up and spoils.

note.label: The water
note.text: Presumably the lilies’ own juice, like the rose juice that spoils rose oil (1.43).

steps.text: Decant it several times into other vessels coated with honey, sprinkling on fine salt and carefully taking off the impurities that collect. This first expression is the finest.

steps.title: Press the petals again
steps.text: Put the pressed petals from the basket back in the basin. Pour on the same amount of aromatised oil as before and add 10 holkai of chopped cardamom. Work it well with your hands, wait a short while, and press it out, cleaning what runs off. This second expression is second in quality.

note.label: Holkai
note.text: The holke is the drachma weight: 10 holkai are 10 drachmas.

steps.text: Pour oil over the petals a third time and do the same, again adding cardamom and salt, coating your hands with honey, and pressing. This last expression is third.

steps.title: A stronger oil
steps.text: Strip another thousand lilies and spread out the petals. Pour the first expression over them and treat them just as the first, mixing in cardamom; then press them out. Treat the second and third expressions the same way, with cardamom. The more often you steep fresh lilies in it, the stronger the perfume.

note.label: Two kinds of repeat
note.text: Pressing the same petals again (step 5) gives lower grades; fresh lilies steeped in the first expression (step 6) make it stronger.

steps.title: Finish with spices
steps.text: At the end, when it seems strong enough, mix into each preparation 2 drachmas of good myrrh, 2 drachmas of cinnamon and 10 drachmas of saffron.

note.label: Each preparation
note.text: The text does not say whether this means each grade or each batch.

They do the same with the second and third expressions.

recipes.greek: ἔνιοι δὲ τὸ ἁπλοῦν ἐξ ἐλαίου βαλανίνου ἢ ἄλλου καὶ 5 κρίνου σκευάζουσι. δοκεῖ δὲ διαφέρειν τὸ ἐν Φοινίκῃ καὶ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ γινόμενον· ἄριστον δέ ἐστιν αὐτοῦ τὸ ὄζον κρίνων. δύναμιν δὲ ἔχει θερμαντικήν, μαλακτικήν, ἀναστομωτικὴν τῶν περὶ μήτραν μύσεων καὶ φλεγμονῶν, καὶ καθόλου πάντων ἐστὶ χρησιμώτατον πρὸς τὰ γυναικεῖα. ἁρμόζει δὲ καὶ πρὸς ἀχῶρας, ἰόνθους, πίτυρα, ἐκζέματα, μώλωπάς τε ταχέως μεταβάλλει καὶ ὁμόχρους ποιεῖ, καὶ καθόλου ἐστὶν ἀραιωτικόν. ἄγει δὲ καὶ χολὴν κατὰ κοιλίαν πινόμενον, κινεῖ δὲ καὶ οὔρησιν. ἐστι δὲ κακοστόμαχον καὶ ναυτίας ποιητικόν.
recipes.english: 5. Some prepare the simple form from balanos oil or another oil and lily. The product made in Phoenicia and Egypt is considered superior; the finest is the one that smells of lilies. It has a warming, softening, and opening capacity for occlusions and inflammations in the region of the uterus and, in general, is among the most useful remedies for women’s complaints. It is also suitable for scaly sores, pimples, dandruff, and skin eruptions. It quickly disperses bruises and restores them to the color of the surrounding skin; in general, it has a rarefying action. When drunk, it also carries bile down through the bowels and promotes urination. It is harmful to the stomach and causes nausea.

recipes.greek: ναρκίσσινον δὲ στύψεις οὕτως· ἐλαίου πεπλυμένου λίτρας ἐννέα οὐγγίας πέντε, ἀσπαλάθου λίτρας ἓξ οὐγγίας δύο κόψας καὶ βρέξας ὕδατι. τῷ τρίτῳ τοῦ ἐλαίου μείξας ἕψε, εἶτα ἐξελὼν τὸν ἀσπάλαθον καὶ καλάμου λίτρας πέντε οὐγγίας ὀκτὼ καὶ σμύρνης χόνδρον κόψας καὶ σήσας φύρα οἴνῳ παλαιῷ εὐώδει καὶ μείξας ἕψε. ὅταν δὲ καὶ μετὰ τούτων ἀναζέσῃ, ἐξελὼν ἀπήθει τὸ ἔλαιον ψυγέν, εἶτα λαβὼν ἐκ τοῦ ἐλαίου [lacuna] [lacuna] εἰς λουτῆρα ἀπόχει καὶ τοῦ ναρκίσσου ἔμβαλε ὡς ὅτι πλεῖστον τὸ ἄνθος, ἐπὶ ἡμέρας δύο κινῶν ὡς ἐπὶ τοῦ σουσίνου, ἐξίπου τε καὶ μετάγγιζε πυκνῶς· καὶ γὰρ τοῦτο σήπεται. ποιεῖ δὲ πρὸς τὰ ἐν ὑστέρᾳ, μαλάσσον τὰς περὶ αὐτὴν σκληρίας καὶ μύσεις. ἔστι δὲ κεφαλαλγές.
recipes.english: Prepare the astringent base for narcissus unguent as follows. Take nine litrai and five ounces of washed oil, and six litrai and two ounces of aspalathos, chopped and soaked in water. Combine the aspalathos with a third of the oil and subject it to boiling. Then remove the aspalathos. Pound and sieve five litrai and eight ounces of calamus together with a lump of myrrh; work them with fragrant old wine, incorporate the mixture into the oil, and boil it. When the oil has boiled up with these ingredients as well, remove it from the heat and strain it after it has cooled. Next, take from the oil [lacuna] [lacuna], decant it into a basin, and put in the greatest possible quantity of narcissus blossom. Stir for two days, as with lily unguent, then press it out and decant it frequently, for this too is liable to spoil. It is effective for disorders of the uterus, softening the indurations and closures around it; but it causes headache.

recipes.english:
To prepare saffron unguent, first make the oil astringent, as stated for susinum, using the same quantity and the same proportion by weight.   Take three and a half litrai of the oil made astringent for lily unguent, add fifty drachmai of saffron, and stir it several times each day for five consecutive days. On the sixth day, strain the oil cleanly from the saffron. Pour the same quantity of oil over that same saffron and stir for ten days. Then pour off the oil, mix in forty drachmai of myrrh that has been pounded and sifted, stir it thoroughly in a mortar, and put it away. Some also use oil perfumed for henna unguent in making saffron unguent. The best kind is intensely fragrant with saffron and is the one suited to medical use; the second-best has a perceptible scent of myrrh.

2. It has a heating and sleep-inducing capacity. It has therefore often proved suitable for patients with phrenitis, either applied in soaked compresses or inhaled and smeared on the nostrils. It also promotes suppuration and cleanses ulcers. It is used for indurations and closures in the uterus and for malignant conditions there, together with wax, saffron, marrow, and twice as much oil; for it brings to coction, softens, soothes, and moistens. When applied with water, it is also effective against blue-gray opacities of the eyes. The unguents called onychinon, boutyrinon, and styrakinon correspond to it: although their names differ, they are similar in preparation and capacity.

recipes.english:
For the astringency and preparation of henna oil, take one part thoroughly washed omphacine oil and one and a half parts rainwater. Pour some of the water over the oil, and work the rest into the aromatics that are to be added. Then take five and a half litrai of aspalathus, six and a half litrai of calamus, one litra of myrrh, three litrai nine oungiai of cardamom, and nine litrai five oungiai of oil. Chop the aspalathus, put it into water to soak, and boil it with the oil until they boil up together. Dissolve the myrrh in fragrant old wine and work the chopped calamus into the myrrh mixture. Remove the aspalathus and add the calamus mixture.

Once it too has boiled with the oil, take the vessel off the heat, strain the oil out of the bronze cauldron, and pour it over the cardamom, which has been chopped and worked together with the remaining water. Stir continuously with a spatula until it cools. Then strain the oil and, for every twenty-eight litrai of oil, add forty-six litrai eight oungiai of henna blossom. Leave it to steep thoroughly, then press it out through a basket. If you want a further steeping, add an equal quantity of fresh blossom and press it out in the same way; thus you may make it double-steeped or triple-steeped, as you wish. It becomes more potent in this way.

One should select a good product with a penetrating fragrance. Some also mix in cinnamon. It has a heating, softening, and opening capacity, suitable for disorders of the womb and sinews, pleurisy, and fractures, whether it is used on its own or mixed with a cerate. It is also mixed into emollient preparations suited to opisthotonos, quinsy, and inflammation of the groin, and into fatigue-relieving preparations.

1. Astringency of iris unguent. Chop six litrai and eight oungiai of spathe as finely as possible. Mix it with nine litrai and five oungiai of oil and ten kotylai of water, put the mixture into a bronze vessel, and boil it until the oil takes on the fragrance. Then strain it into a mixing bowl coated with honey. From this aromatized oil the first iris unguent is prepared by steeping iris in the astringent oil, as set out below. […] 3. In fragrance, the best kind is that which smells of iris alone and of nothing else. Such is the kind made at Perge in Pamphylia and at Elis in Achaea. It has an emollient and warming capacity. It thoroughly cleanses eschars, putrefactions, and filth, and is suitable for conditions affecting the uterus, including inflammations and closures. It also expels embryos and opens hemorrhoids. For sounds heard in the ears, it is used together with vinegar, rue, and bitter almonds. It is also suitable for persistent catarrhs, when the nostrils are anointed with it, and for ozena.

4. When one kyathos is drunk, it also purges the bowels, helps in ileus-like conditions, and promotes urination. It is also suitable for those who vomit only with difficulty, when either the fingers or the emetic agents are smeared with it; for those suffering from synanche, when it is applied as an ointment or gargled with melikraton; and for roughness of the windpipe. It is also administered when hemlock, mushrooms, or coriander have been swallowed.

recipes.greek: ἀμαράκινον δὲ ἐν Κυζίκῳ κάλλιστον γίνεται. σκευάζεται δὲ διά τε ὀμφακίνου ἐλαίου καὶ βαλανίνου, στυφομένων ξυλοβαλσάμῳ, σχοίνῳ, καλάμῳ, ἡδυνομένων δὲ ἀμαράκῳ, κόστῳ, ἀμώμῳ, νάρδῳ, κασσίᾳ, καρπῷ βαλσάμου καὶ σμύρνῃ. οἱ δὲ πολυτελέστερον αὐτὸ ποιοῦντες μίσγουσι καὶ κινάμωμον· παραλαμβάνεται δὲ μέλι καὶ οἶνος εἰς τὴν τῶν ἀγγείων χρίσιν καὶ φύραδιν τῶν κεκομμένων ἀρωμάτων. ἐστι δὲ θερμαντικόν, καρωτικόν, μαλακτικόν, ἀναστομωτικόν, 2 πυρωτικόν, οὐρητικόν, εὐχρηστοῦν εἴς τε τὰς σῆπας καὶ σύριγγας καὶ ὑδροκήλας μετὰ τὰς χειρουργίας, περιρρήττει τε τὰς ἐσχάρας καὶ τὰ τεθηριωμένα ἕλκη, πρός τε δυσουρίαν ἁρμόζει περιχριομένου τοῦ δακτυλίου, καὶ πρὸς τὰς φλεγμονὰς αὐτοῦ καὶ πρὸς αἱμορροίδων ἀναστόμωσιν περιχριόμενον, ἔμμηνά τε κινεῖ προστιθέμενον τῇ μήτρᾳ καὶ σκληρίας καὶ οἰδήματα ἐν ὑστέρᾳ διαφορεῖ, καὶ πρὸς τὰ μυότρωτα καὶ νευρότρωτα συμφέρει ἐν πιλήμασιν ἀραιοῖς βρεχόμενον καὶ ἐπιτιθέμενον.
recipes.english:
The finest marjoram unguent is made at Cyzicus. It is prepared from both omphacine oil and balanus oil, made astringent with balsam wood, schoenus, and calamus, and perfumed with marjoram, costus, amomum, nard, cassia, balsam fruit, and myrrh. Those who make it more costly also add cinnamon. Honey and wine are employed both to coat the vessels and to knead the chopped aromatics.

It has heating, stupor-inducing, softening, opening, burning, and diuretic effects. After surgical procedures, it is useful for putrefactions, fistulas, and hydroceles. It breaks open eschars and malignant ulcers. For difficulty in urination, it is suitable when smeared around the anus; it is also applied for inflammation of the anus and, when smeared around hemorrhoids, opens them. It sets menstruation in motion when applied to the womb and disperses indurations and swellings in the womb. It also benefits wounds of the muscles and sinews when pieces of loosely felted wool are soaked in it and applied.

recipes.greek: 3 τὸ δὲ μεγάλλειον καλούμενον πάλαι μέν ποτε ἐσκευάζετο, ἐκλέλοιπε δὲ νῦν. πρὸς ἐκπλήρωσιν δὲ τῆς ἱστορίας οὐκ ἐστιν ἄτοπον ἐπιμνησθῆναι καὶ τούτου. δὲ σκευασία ἡ αὐτὴ τῷ ἀμαρακίνῳ, πλεονάζει δὲ τῇ ῥητίνη καὶ ταύτῃ διαφέρει. ἐστι δὲ μαλακτικὸν ἠπίως. ἡ μέντοι ῥητίνη μείγνυται τοῖς μύροις οὔτε φυλακῆς οὔτε ἡδονῆς χάριν, χρώματος δὲ καὶ πάχους ἕνεκα. μείγνυται δὲ ἠ τερεβινθίνη ἀφεψομένη, ἄχρις ὅτου ἄν ἄοσμος γένηται. δηλωθήσεται δὲ ἐν τοῖς περὶ ῥητίνης (I 71) ἡ ἕψησις αὐτοῦ.
recipes.english: The unguent called Megalleion used to be prepared in former times but has now disappeared. Still, for the sake of completeness, it is appropriate to mention it as well. Its preparation is the same as that of marjoram unguent, except that it contains a greater proportion of resin; this is the point of difference. It has a mildly softening effect. Resin, however, is mixed into unguents neither to preserve them nor to make them pleasant, but to impart color and thickness. Terebinth resin is added after being boiled down until it becomes odorless. The method of boiling it will be explained in the section on resin (I 71).

recipes.summary: An Egyptian unguent, named for its galbanum: the wood that galbanum comes from is called metopon. It is compounded from bitter almonds, unripe-olive oil, cardamom, schoinos, calamus, honey, wine, myrrh, balsam fruit, galbanum and resin; no amounts or method are given.
recipes.greek: σκευάζεται δὲ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ μύρον, ἐπιχωρίως ὑπʼ αὐτῶν καλούμενον μετώπιον διὰ τὴν τῆς χαλβάνης μεῖξιν· τὸ γὰρ ξύλον, ἐξ οὗ γεννᾶται ἡ χαλβάνη, μέτωπον καλεῖται. διʼ ἀμυγδάλων δὲ πικρῶν καὶ ἐλαίου ὀμφακίνου καὶ καρδαμώμου καὶ σχοίνου καὶ καλάμου καὶ μέλιτος καὶ οἴνου καὶ σμύρνης καὶ βαλσάμου καρποῦ καὶ χαλβάνης καὶ ῥητίνης συντίθεται. δόκιμον δέ ἐστι τὸ βαρύοσμον καὶ λιπαρόν, ἐμφαῖνον μᾶλλον τοῦ καρδαμώμου καὶ τῆς σμύρνης ἤπερ τῆς χαλβάνης. 2 σφόδρα δὲ θερμαίνει καὶ πυροῖ καὶ ἀναστομοῖ ἐπισπᾶταί τε καὶ καθαίρει ἕλκη, πρός τε νεῦρα καὶ μύας διακοπέντα ποιεῖ, ὑδροκήλας τε σὺν σηπταῖς. μείγνυται δὲ καὶ μαλάγμασι καὶ κηρωταῖς, πρός τε ῥίγη καὶ ὀπισθοτονικῶς σπωμένους χρησιμεύει. κινεῖ δὲ καὶ ἱδρῶτας καὶ ἀναστομοῖ τὰ περὶ ὑστέραν καὶ σκληρίας τὰς περὶ αὐτὴν χαλᾷ, καὶ καθόλου μαλακτικὴν ἔχει τὴν δύναμιν.
recipes.english:
In Egypt an unguent is prepared which the inhabitants call metopion, because galbanum is mixed into it: the wood from which galbanum is produced is called metopon. It is compounded from bitter almonds, oil of unripe olives, cardamom, camel hay, sweet flag, honey, wine, myrrh, balsam fruit, galbanum, and resin. A satisfactory specimen has a heavy scent and an oily consistency, with cardamom and myrrh more evident than galbanum.

It heats strongly, produces burning heat, opens passages, draws, and cleanses ulcers. It is effective for severed sinews and muscles, and for hydroceles accompanied by putrefaction. It is also mixed into emollient plasters and cerates, and is useful against chills and for people suffering opisthotonic spasms. It induces sweating, opens the passages around the uterus, and relaxes indurations there; in general, it has an emollient capacity.

recipes.greek: κιναμώμινον δὲ ἔκ τε ἐλαίου βαλανίνου καὶ στυμμάτων ξυλοβαλσάμου, καλάμου, σχοίνου, ἡδυσμάτων δὲ κιναμώμου, βαλσάμου καρποῦ, σμύρνης τετραπλασίονος παράὰ τὸ κινάμωμον σκευάζεται· μείγνυται δὲ καὶ μέλι εἰς τὴν φύρασιν. δόκιμον δέ ἐστι τὸ μὴ δριμύ, μαλακὸν δὲ τῇ ὀσμῇ καὶ παρεμφαῖνον σμύρνης, παχύ τε καὶ εὐῶδες ἄγαν, τῇ γεύσει πικρόν. τὸ γὰρ τοιοῦτον οὐκ ἐκ ῥητίνης ἀλλʼ ἐκ σμύρνης ἔχει τὸ πάχος· ἡ γὰρ ῥητίνη οὐ προσδίδωσι πικρίαν οὐδὲ εὐωδίαν. δύναμιν δὲ ἔχει σφόδρα δριμεῖαν καὶ θερμαντικὴν καὶ 2 πικράν. ἀναστομοῖ γοῦν θερμαῖνον καὶ διαφορεῖ καὶ διαχεῖ καὶ ἐπισπᾶται ὑγρὰ καὶ πνεύματα· ἔστι δὲ καρηβαρικόν. ποιεῖ δὲ καὶ πρὸς τὰ περὶ μήτραν σὺν ἐλαίῳ διπλασίονι καὶ κηρῷ καὶ μυελῷ. οὕτως γὰρ ἀποβάλλει τὸ πολὺ τῆς δριμύτητος καὶ γίνεται μαλακτικόν· ἄλλως γὰρ συγκαίει καὶ σκληρύνει βιαιότατα πάντων τῶν παχέων μύρων. ποιεῖ καὶ τρὸς σύριγγας καὶ σῆ πας ἐναργῶς καὶ πρὸς ὑδροκήλας καὶ ἄνθρακας καὶ γαγγραίνας σὺν καρδαμώμῳ, πρός τε ῥίγη τὰ περιοδικὰ καὶ πρὸς τρόμους καὶ τοὺς ὑπὸ τῶν ἰοβόλων θηρίων δακνομένους ἐν συγχρίσματι, ἐπίθεμά τε σκορπιοπλήκτοις καὶ φαλαγγιοδήκτοις σὺν ὀλύνθοις λείοις.
recipes.english:
Cinnamon unguent is prepared from ben oil; astringent ingredients consisting of balsam wood, sweet flag, and camel hay; and aromatic ingredients consisting of cinnamon, balsam fruit, and four times as much myrrh as cinnamon. Honey is also mixed in during the kneading. A satisfactory specimen is not acrid but mild in scent, with a suggestion of myrrh; it is thick, intensely fragrant, and bitter to the taste. Such an unguent derives its thickness not from resin but from myrrh, since resin contributes neither bitterness nor fragrance.

Its capacity is intensely acrid, warming, and bitter. Accordingly, as it warms, it opens passages, disperses, diffuses, and draws fluids and pneuma toward itself; but it causes heaviness in the head. Mixed with twice as much oil, together with wax and marrow, it is also effective for disorders around the uterus. In this form it loses much of its acridity and becomes emollient; otherwise it burns and hardens more violently than any other thick unguent. With cardamom it is manifestly effective for fistulas and putrefactions, hydroceles, carbuncles, and gangrenes. As an ointment it is also effective against recurrent chills and tremors and for people bitten by venomous animals; mixed with finely ground unripe figs, it is applied as a poultice to those stung by scorpions or bitten by venomous spiders.

recipes.summary: Nard unguent is made in various ways, with or without malabathron leaf. Most often ben oil or oil of unripe olives is made astringent with camel hay and scented with costus, amomum, nard, myrrh and balsam. A plain version uses unripe-olive oil, camel hay, sweet flag, costus and nard.
recipes.greek: νάρδινον δὲ μύρον ποικίλως σκευάζεται διὰ τοῦ μαλαβαθρίνου φύλλου καὶ δίχα τούτου. ὡς τὸ πολὺ δὲ μείγνυται τῷ βαλανίνῳ ἐλαίῳ ἢ ὀμφακίνῳ, πρὸς μὲν τὴν στύψιν τοῦ ἐλαίου σχοῖνος, πρὸς δὲ τὴν εὐωδίαν βάλλεται κόστος, ἄμωμον, νάρδος, σμύρνα, βάλσαμον. ἐστι δὲ χρηστὴ ἡ λεπτή, μὴ δριμεῖα, ἔχουσα τὴν εὐωδίαν τῆς ξηρᾶς νάρδου ἢ ἀμώμου. δύναμις δὲ αὐτῆς λεπτυντική, δριμεῖα, σμηκτική, θερμαντική. ὑγρὰ δέ ἐστι καὶ οὐ γλοιώδης, ἐὰν μὴ ῥητίνην ἔχῃ. σκευάζεται δὲ καὶ λιτὴ δι᾿ ὀμφακίνου ἐλαίου καὶ σχοίνου καὶ καλάμου καὶ κόστου καὶ νάρδου.
recipes.english: Nard unguent is prepared in various ways, either with malabathron leaf or without it. Most commonly it is compounded with ben oil or oil of unripe olives. Camel hay is added to impart astringency to the oil, while costus, amomum, nard, myrrh, and balsam are added for fragrance. A good specimen is thin and not acrid, and has the fragrance of dried nard or amomum. Its capacity is attenuating, acrid, cleansing, and warming. It is fluid rather than glutinous unless it contains resin. A plain version is also prepared from oil of unripe olives, camel hay, sweet flag, costus, and nard.

recipes.summary: A Persian oil called iasme: two ounces of the white flowers of the violet are steeped in an Italian xestes of sesame oil and replaced with fresh ones, as for lily oil.
recipes.greek: ἡ δὲ καλουμένη ἰάσμη παρὰ Πέρσαις σκευάζεται ἐκ τῶν ἀνθῶν τῶν λευκῶν τοῦ ἰοῦ, τούτων οὐγγίων βʹ ἐμβαλλομένων Ἰταλικῷ ξέστῃ σησαμίνου ἐλαίου καὶ ἀμειβομένων ἤγουν ἀλλασσομένων ὡς ἐπὶ τοῦ κρινίνου εἴρηται. ἡ δὲ τούτου χρῆσις παρὰ τὰς ἑστιάσεις εὐωδίας ἕνεκα παρὰ Πέρσαις παραλαμβάνεται. ἁρμόζει δὲ καὶ ὅλῳ τῷ σώματι κατὰ τὰ λουτρὰ ἐπὶ τῶι θερμασίας καὶ χαλάσεως δεομένων σωμάτων. βαρυτέραν δὲ ἔχει τὴν εὐωδίαν, ὡς πολλοὺς αὐτῆς μηδὲ (μή p) ἡδέως ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι

title.source: Every liquid resin is processed by heating

recipes.summary: Liquid resin, first strained while melted, is boiled gently with twice its measure of rainwater in a bronze vessel over coals, stirring all the time, until it is odourless, crumbly and dry. It is then cooled and stored in an unpitched earthenware vessel; it comes out very white.

recipes.greek: καίεται δὲ πᾶσα ῥητίνη ὑγρὰ ἐν τετραπλασίονι ἀγγείῳ 5 κατὰ τὸ τοῦ ἐγχεομένου ὑγροῦ πλῆθος· δεῖ γὰρ χοῦν μὲν τῆς ῥητίνης, δύο δὲ χοέας ὀμερίου ὕδατος ἐμβαλόντας εἰς χαλκεῖον ἕψειν ἐπʼ ἀνθράκων πραέως, διηνεκῶς κινοῦντας, ἄχρις οὗ ἄνοσμος γένηται καὶ εὔθρυπτος καὶ καπυρά, ὡς μὴ τοῖς δακτύλοις εἴκειν, λοιπὸν δὲ ψύξαντας εἰς κεραμεοῦν ἀγγεῖον ἀκώνητον [τουτέστιν ἀπίσσωτον] ἀποτίθεσθαι. γίνεται δὲ ἐξόχως λευκή· δεῖ μέντοι προδιυλίζειν πᾶσαν ῥητίνην τήκοντας, ἵνα χωρισθῇ τὸ ῥυπῶδες αὐτῆς.

Put one chous of resin and two choes of rainwater into a bronze vessel and boil gently over coals, stirring continuously, until it becomes odorless, readily crumbled, and so thoroughly dry that it no longer yields to the fingers. Then let it cool and store it in an untreated earthenware vessel [that is, an unpitched vessel]. It becomes exceptionally white. Every resin must first be strained while being melted, however, so that its dirt is separated out.

recipes.summary: Resins can also be boiled without water: gently over coals at first, then, when they begin to thicken, over a large heap of coals, without a break for three days and three nights, until they reach the state described for resin boiled with water. Dry resins need only one full day.

recipes.greek: 6 καίονται δὲ καὶ δίχα ὕδατος ἐπ᾿ ἀνθράκων κούφως τὸ πρῶτον· ὅταν δὲ μέλλωσι συστρέφειν, ἀθρόως [καὶ] πολλοὺς ὑποθετέον τοὺς ἄνθρακας καὶ ἑψητέον ἀδιαλείπτως ἐπὶ ἡμέρας καὶ νύκτας τρεῖς, ἄχρι ἂν τὸ προειρημένον ἰδίωμα ἀπολάβωσιν· ἀποτίθεσο δέ, ὡς εἵρηται. τὰς μέντοι ξηρὰς ἀρκέσει διʼ ὅλης ἡμέρας ἑψήσαντας ἀποτίθεσθαι. εὐχρηστοῦσι δὲ αἱ κεκαυμέναι εἴς τε τὰ εὐώδη τῶν μαλαγμάτων καὶ ἄκοπα καὶ εἰς χρωματισμοὺς μύρων. ἐκλαμβάνεται δὲ καὶ λιγνὺς ῥητίνης, ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τοῦ λιβάνου, ἥτις χρησιμεύει πρός τε καλλιβλέφαρα καὶ περιβεβρωμένους κανθοὺς καὶ μυδῶντα βλέφαρα καὶ δακρύοντας ὀφθαλμούς. γίνεται δὲ ἐξ αὐτῆς καὶ μέλαν, ᾧ γράφομεν.
recipes.english: 6. Resins are also processed over coals without water, gently at first. When they are about to thicken, place coals beneath them all at once [and] in large quantity, and boil without interruption for three days and three nights, until they acquire the quality described above; then store them as stated. For dry resins, however, it will suffice to boil them for one full day before storing them. Resins processed in this way are useful for imparting fragrance to emollient applications, for fatigue-relieving remedies, and for coloring perfumed oils. Resin soot is also collected in the same way as frankincense soot. It is useful for eyelid cosmetics, eroded corners of the eyes, moist and suppurating eyelids, and watering eyes. It is also used to make the ink with which we write.

recipes.summary: The simple rose oil: red rose petals, their bases removed and aired for a day and a night, are sealed in a jar with unripe-olive oil and left outdoors in the sun for forty days. Some keep the jar in a well or bury it instead.

time.note: No temperatures are given. In the well method the jar stays down for the same forty days.

recipes.greek: Ῥόδων ἐρυθρῶν ὠνυχισμένων καὶ διεψυγμένων νυχθήμερον α 𐆄 γ, ἐλαίου ὀμφακίνου ξ̸ Ἰταλικὸν α· περισφίγξας ἐπιμελῶς τὸν βῖκον, ὡς μὴ διαπνεῖσθαι, ἡλίου ἐν ὑπαίθρῳ ἐπὶ μ ἡμέρας καὶ τότε ἀποτίθεσο μὴ ἐπ' ἐδάφους ἀλλ' ἐπὶ σανίδος. τινὲς δὲ ἀντὶ τῆς ἡλιώσεως καθίασιν εἰς φρέαρ τὸν βῖκον τὰς μ ἡμέρας διὰ τὸ ἐκ τῆς ψύξεως διαφυλαχθῆναι τὴν εὐωδίαν, ἄλλοι δὲ κατορύττουσιν αὐτὸν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς.
recipes.english: Take three ounces of red rose petals whose nail-like bases have been removed and which have been aired for a day and a night, and one Italian sextarius of unripe-olive oil. Seal the jar carefully so that its contents do not evaporate, and leave it outdoors in the sun for forty days. Then store it on a plank rather than on the ground. Instead of sunning the jar, some lower it into a well for the forty days, so that the cold preserves the fragrance; others bury it in the earth.

time.note: No temperatures are given beyond rooms of even temperature for storing. In the well method the jar stays down forty days.

recipes.greek: Ῥόδινον σκευάζεται οὕτως· ῥόδων ἐρυθρῶν ἐξωνυχισμένων καὶ ἐψυγμένων ἡμέραν καὶ νύκτα 𐆄 γ, ἐλαίου ὀμφακίνου ξέστης ἰταλικὸς εἷς, ἐμβάλλοντα δὲ τὰ ῥόδα περισφίγγειν χρὴ τὸ στόμα τοῦ βίκου ἔσωθεν μὲν ὀθονίῳ, ἔξωθεν δὲ δέρματι διὰ τοὺς γιγνομένους ὄμβρους αἰφνίδιον καὶ ἡλιοῦν ἡμέρας κ καὶ οὕτως σειρώσαντα ἀποτίθεσθαι τοὺς βίκους ἐπὶ σανίδων ἐν οἴκοις εὐκράτοις. τινὲς δὲ ἕτερά τινα προσεμβάλλουσι τοῖς ῥόδοις. ἀρίστη δέ ἐστιν ἡ διὰ τῶν ῥόδων μόνων καὶ ἐλαίου σκευασία. τινὲς δὲ οὐχ ἡλιοῦσιν, ἀλλ' ἀποκρημνοῦσι τὸν βίκον εἰς φρέαρ ὕδατος ψυχροῦ ἡμέρας μ. ἁρμόζει δὲ κεφαλῇ θερμανθείσῃ καὶ ξηρανθείσῃ ἢ ἐξ ἡλιώσεως ἢ ἐκ πυρετῶν ἤ τινος ἄλλης τοιαύτης προφάσεως. ὑγραίνει γὰρ καὶ παρηγορεῖ καὶ ὕπνον ἐπάγει. […] καὶ πινόμενον δὲ τὸ κάλλιστον ῥόδινον σὺν ὕδατι ψυχρῷ ἢ θερμῷ ἐπὶ τῶν δακνομένων τὸν στόμαχον ἐκ χολῆς δριμείας ἢ ἐλμίνθων ἢ ἀσκαρίδων μεγάλας παρέχει ὠφελείας. ἐπὶ δὲ ἐλμίνθων καὶ μάλιστα ἐπὶ παίδων κρεῖττον ποιεῖ μιγνύμενον ἑψήματι τῷ ἀπ' οἴνου τριτουμένου σκευαζομένῳ καὶ πινόμενον· ἐκτινάσσει γὰρ αὐτὰς τάχιστα. ἐνίεται δὲ καὶ κώλῳ δακνομένῳ διὰ τὰς εἰρημένας προφάσεις. παραφυλακτέον δὲ τὴν χρῆσιν αὐτοῦ ἐφ' ὧν μὴ πολλή ἐστιν ἡ θερμασία καὶ περιττὸν τὸ σῶμα.
recipes.english: Rose oil is prepared as follows: take three unciae of red roses with the calyces removed and cooled for a day and a night, and one Italian sextarius of omphakine oil. When the roses are put in, the mouth of the jar must be tied shut, inside with linen and outside with hide because sudden showers may occur, and it should be exposed to the sun for twenty days. After straining it, set the jars on boards in rooms of even temperature. Some people add other ingredients to the roses, but preparation from roses alone and oil is best. Some do not expose it to the sun, but lower the jar into a well of cold water for forty days. It is suitable for a head that has become hot and dry from sun exposure, fevers, or some other similar cause, for it moistens, soothes, and brings on sleep. […] The finest rose oil, when drunk with cold or warm water, gives great benefit to people whose stomach is bitten by sharp bile, intestinal worms, or large roundworms. For worms, especially in children, it works better when mixed with a decoction prepared from wine diluted to one-third strength and drunk, for it expels them very quickly. It is also injected into the colon when it is being bitten for the causes already mentioned. Its use must be avoided in patients where there is not much heat and the body has excess.

ingredients.note: Red roses, the calyces removed, cooled for a day and a night.
Omphakine oil, from unripe olives.
ingredients.flag: Italian sextarius taken to be the xestes of units.json (0.547 l)
ingredients.name: Unripe-olive oil

steps.title: Prepare the roses
steps.text: Take three unciae of red roses. Remove the calyces and leave them to cool for a day and a night.

note.label: Calyces removed
note.text: The Greek ἐξωνυχισμένων is the word Paul uses (ὠνυχισμένων), which his translation renders "nail-like bases removed".

steps.title: Add the oil and seal
steps.text: Put the roses into a jar with one Italian sextarius of omphakine oil. Tie the mouth of the jar shut, inside with linen and outside with hide, in case of sudden showers.

steps.title: Sun
steps.text: Set the jar in the sun for twenty days.

note.label: Twenty days
note.text: Paul (7.20.4) gives forty days in the sun for the same oil.

steps.title: Strain and store
steps.text: Strain it, then set the jars on boards in rooms of even temperature.

other_ways.title: In a well
other_ways.text: Some do not sun it, but lower the jar into a well of cold water for forty days.

other_ways.title: With other ingredients
other_ways.text: Some add other ingredients to the roses, but roses and oil alone make the best preparation.

text: Roses and oil alone make the best preparation.

recipes.uses: For a head made hot and dry by sun, fever or the like: it moistens, soothes and brings on sleep; the finest, drunk with cold or warm water, for a stomach bitten by sharp bile or worms; with a wine decoction, against worms, especially in children; injected into the colon; not to be used where there is little heat and the body has excess.

uses_items.note: cold or warm water, drunk with the finest rose oil
a decoction 'prepared from wine diluted to one-third strength' (approved English), mixed with the oil and drunk against worms

notes: Olivieri's Greek is printed in lines with line-end hyphens; the lines are joined here by script (line-end hyphens removed, other line breaks turned into spaces).
The chapter heading Ἔλαιον ῥόδινον, κηρωτὴ ἡ ψύχουσα ('Rose oil; the cooling wax-salve.') is left out, since it names the wax-salve too; the text starts at Ῥόδινον σκευάζεται οὕτως.

[…] marks an omission in both Greek and English: the cooling wax-salve (κηρωτή) made with the oil, from καὶ ἐπὶ σπλάγχνων to τοῦ ε λόγου (perfume-tables keeps it as aetius-1-113-2), and Olivieri's bracketed doublet [πλυνομένη … σπλάγχνοις]. The closing passage on drinking the finest rose oil (τὸ κάλλιστον ῥόδινον) is kept as part of the oil's uses.
Some add other ingredients to the roses; the text says roses and oil alone make the best preparation.
The Italian sextarius (ξέστης ἰταλικός) is taken to be the xestes of units.json.
Twenty days in the sun (κ) here against forty in Paul 7.20.4 (μ); the well alternative is forty days in both.
Plain step 6 (the well instead of the sun) is moved to other_ways; plain steps 4 and 5 (strain, store) are merged.
